title: Temperance
hookLine: enough, not too much: joy in good things rightly used

cards: Honey. Proverbs has advice about it, and it's surprisingly practical: "Hast thou found honey? eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it." No lecture about sugar.
No claim that honey is bad. In fact the verse assumes you'll find some, and eat some. It just knows the moment when the next spoonful turns sweet into sick.
Anyone who has finished a whole bag of something at midnight knows that moment too. Today, the last of the four cardinal virtues, the one that knows where that line is.

teach.b: Start with what temperance is not. It isn't a suspicion of good things. A psalm thanks God for "wine that maketh glad the heart of man," and bread that strengthens the heart.
Ecclesiastes says that to eat and drink and enjoy the good of your work "is the gift of God."
And the first letter to Timothy says it outright: "every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." So temperance starts with yes.
Good food, good drink, rest, screens, shopping, work: gifts.
Temperance is the skill of enjoying them at the right measure, so they stay gifts and don't become masters.
Paul lists it among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians: love, joy, peace, and on through the list, ending with "meekness, temperance: against such there is no law."
The Greek word there is enkrateia, self-mastery, being in charge of your own appetite instead of the other way around.
The Book of Wisdom's list of four uses a different Greek word, sophrosyne, soundness of mind; the King James calls both temperance. And it's called fruit.
Some Christian teachers speak of it as something that grows in a person, not a rule clamped on from outside. Churches apply it differently. Some ask members not to drink alcohol at all.
Others drink in moderation and use wine at communion. Both are trying to keep good things in their place. Too much honey isn't more joy.
Stopping at enough is how the joy survives.

how: Some Christians practice temperance through grace before meals, fasting seasons such as Lent, and moderation in food, drink and pleasures; some churches ask members to abstain from alcohol, while others drink in moderation and use wine at communion.

o: a calm, even mood that never gets upset
holding back every feeling that you have
enjoying good things at the right measure

p: eat so much as is sufficient
wine that maketh glad the heart

s: the Bible treats good food and drink as suspicious
"every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving."
Paul lists temperance as a fruit of the Spirit
Galatians 5 ends the list with "meekness, temperance."
Proverbs tells you never to eat honey
it says to eat what is sufficient for you, and stop there.

games.q: you've found honey, and it's very good. the jar is still half full. what does Proverbs advise?
o: throw it out; sweet things are a trap.
eat so much as is sufficient for you.
finish it now, while it's good.
games.why: "eat so much as is sufficient for thee, lest thou be filled therewith, and vomit it." the honey is good. the measure keeps it good.

practice: Think of one good thing you tend to keep going with past the point of joy, scrolling, snacking, a show that rolls into the next one, and picture the moment it's good, then the moment it tips, the spoonful too many.
Notice, gently, where that line sits for you. If you pray, you can give thanks for the good thing itself.

wordCard.voice: Temperance. Joy in good things at the right measure. In Paul's Greek, enkrateia: being master of your appetite, not mastered by it.

orig.note: Greek: self-mastery, self-control; the word translated temperance in Galatians 5:23.

carryVoice: Your line: enough is joy. The good thing stays good when you stop. Twelve hundred days now.
